diagnostic_signals.reading: Available OECD price comparison places US health-sector prices about 27 percent above the OECD average; OECD cautions that methodological differences may understate the US level.

diagnostic_signals.comparison_scope: United States versus other G7 average
diagnostic_signals.reading: Price-adjusted health-goods-and-services volume was estimated at about 1.6 times the other-G7 average, versus spending at about 2.2 times; selected imaging and elective procedures were elevated, but physician and bed supply was not.

diagnostic_signals.comparison_scope: United States versus other G7 average
diagnostic_signals.reading: Administration accounted for about 8 percent of US health spending and more than USD 800 per person, over five times the other-G7 per-person average.

diagnostic_signals.period: latest values in OECD 2025 country note
diagnostic_signals.comparison_scope: United States versus OECD average where available
diagnostic_signals.reading: Core-service coverage was 93 percent. Obesity was 35 percent versus 19 percent OECD average, while smoking was lower; need and risk differ, but OECD analysis finds age structure does not explain the high US spending level.

diagnostic_signals.period: latest values in OECD 2025 country note
diagnostic_signals.reading: Outcomes are mixed: life expectancy was 2.7 years lower and preventable and treatable mortality were higher, while 30-day mortality after heart attack and stroke was lower.

current_growth_context.reading: CMS reports 2024 growth was primarily driven by non-price factors, including demand and service mix. This is a one-year growth decomposition and does not contradict the OECD cross-sectional price signal.

required_next_step: Build same-year service-level price-times-volume comparisons for hospital, physician/clinical, and drug categories with case-mix, quality, access, and coverage floors before estimating an addressable amount.
